75	## 5. Git and pull requests (decision record 0009)
76	
77	- **Branch names:** `<type>/<NN>-<slug>`, where `NN` is the stack number — `feat/03a-apply`, `spec/03b-workbench`.
78	- **Commit messages:** Conventional Commits — `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `docs:`, `chore:`, plus two local types, `spec:` and `adr:`. End agent-written commits with the co-author line your session instructions give you.
79	- **Stacks:** the bottom pull request targets `main`; each one above targets its parent branch — `gh pr create --base <parent-branch>`. At most four deep.
80	- **Pull request body, three headings:** *What* · *Which invariant it satisfies* · *What is deliberately not here*. End with the generated-with line your session instructions give you.
81	- **Merging:** squash, keeping the conventional prefix in the subject. `main` stays green.
82	- **Never commit or push to `main` directly.** Never force-push a branch Kent is reviewing without telling him.
83	
84	### Merging a stack — the method that actually works
85	
86	**`gh pr merge` refuses a stacked pull request.** It errors out because the head branch is not based on the default branch. Use the merge-queue API directly, bottom pull request first:
87	
88	```bash
89	gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async \
90	  -f merge_method=squash \
91	  -f commit_title="<subject> (#<n>)" \
92	  -f commit_message="<the What section of the body>" \
93	  -f sha=<head sha of that branch>
94	```
95	
96	It answers with a job identifier. Poll it until it reports done:
97	
98	```bash
99	gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async/<uuid>
100	```
101	
102	Then move up the stack. Three rules that will save you an hour:
103	
104	1. **Bottom-up, always.** Merge the pull request whose base is `main` first. Merging the top of a stack with `gh pr merge` merges it **into its parent branch**, not into `main` — it looks like it worked and it silently did the wrong thing. Never do it.
105	2. **A child branch that already merged in a sibling stack needs `git merge origin/main` first**, then a push, before its own merge will go through cleanly. This happens whenever two stacks ran in parallel and touched the same file.
106	3. **Delete the branches afterwards** (`gh api -X DELETE repos/kgang/katalyst/git/refs/heads/<branch>`, or the `--delete-branch` flag on the next `gh pr merge` that does work), and remove the worktrees with `git worktree remove`.

129	## 7. The worktree pattern
130	
131	Every sub-agent gets its own checkout of its own branch under **`../katalyst-wt/<branch-slug>/`**. The main checkout stays on `main` and is never used by a sub-agent.
132	
133	```bash
134	git worktree add ../katalyst-wt/feat-03a-apply -b feat/03a-apply <base-branch>
135	```
136	
137	The rules, and they are not negotiable because they are what keeps eight parallel agents from stepping on each other:
138	
139	- **One agent per worktree**, except for chapter writers, who may share one worktree **only** when their files are disjoint and **none of them runs a git command**.
140	- **Disjoint owned files.** Every brief carries an explicit list. "Touch nothing outside it. If you believe something outside it must change, write why in your report and stop."
141	- **Agents never push, never open a pull request, never touch `main`.** They commit on their branch and report. The coordinator reviews, then pushes and opens the pull request.
142	- **Remove worktrees after the merge:** `git worktree remove ../katalyst-wt/<slug>`.

146	## 8. Lessons — read these twice
147	
148	1. **After any interruption, check reality before acting.** Run `git log --oneline -5`, `git status`, `gh pr list`, and read `STATUS.md`. A previous agent lost part of its context mid-session and re-did work that was already committed — overwrote a committed file and launched sub-agents to revise approved text. It was caught and reverted, but only by luck. Do not trust your memory of the repo; trust the repo.
149	2. **Append to `STATUS.md` before you stop**, every time. It is how the next agent — or you, after a context loss — finds the thread.
150	3. **Brief sub-agents fully.** They know only what you tell them. Give each a disjoint set of files. Paste the pre-decisions, never link them: `plans/` is git-ignored and the agent may be in a worktree that cannot see it.
151	4. **Keep cross-references consistent.** One rename touched 26 references across 12 files. After any rename, search the whole repo for the old name.
152	5. **Status lives in three places** for a decision record: its own front-matter, `docs/adr/README.md`, and the table in `ARCHITECTURE.md` §9. Change all three together.
153	6. **Verify every sub-agent's claim yourself.** Run the tests, run the lints, read the diff, look at the screen. Agents flagged real inconsistencies last session and also drifted once (`retune` used for the wrong thing). A report is a hypothesis, not evidence.
154	7. **Write the shapes sheet before the parallel writers start.** The stack 02 shapes sheet is why six chapters and two code agents used the same field names. Without it you get six different answers to the same small question, and the reconciliation costs more than the sheet did.
155	8. **Put a reviewer agent over parallel writers.** The read-only reviewer over the six stack-02 chapters found five blocking problems and about twenty consistency ones before Kent saw a word. It is the cheapest agent you will run.
156	9. **Sub-agents sometimes write the wrong co-author line.** Harmless: every pull request is squash-merged, and the coordinator writes the squash message. Do not spend time correcting it on the branch.
157	10. **The first pull request of a stack is usually small enough to write yourself.** Stack 01's README took twenty minutes of coordinator time and unblocked the next agent immediately. Launching a sub-agent for it would have cost more in briefing than in typing. The same trick works for chapter *stubs*: commit the headings, and the code agent can branch off the spec branch before the chapters are written.

130	### The time axis
131	
132	Day zero is `as_of`. The window runs from day zero to the latest resolve-by date on the map, in whole days. Every date becomes an integer day index at the edge of this function and stays an integer inside it.
133	
134	**When a claim is settled, which is not the same as whether it is true.** Every claim gets a day on which it is settled — the day its clock starts, so that any arrow leaving it measures elapsed days from there. If an assignment fixes it, that day is the assignment's `at` (day zero when `at` is `None`). Otherwise it is the earliest day any live incoming arrow reaches it: the day that arrow's source was settled, plus the arrow's `lag`. A claim with neither an assignment nor a live incoming arrow is settled on **day zero** — the map carries no timing information about it, so its clock starts at the beginning of the window.
135	
136	**Being settled says nothing about being true.** A claim with no assignment is sampled from its own `prior`, every draw, exactly as always; nothing is ever forced true because its clock started. The two ideas are separate and conflating them is the mistake this paragraph exists to prevent. It follows that `t_source` — when each claim was settled — is a **schedule computed once from the shape of the map**, the same in every draw, while **truth is per draw**: an arrow's term is non-zero only in those draws where its source came out true. One schedule, sixteen thousand different worlds running along it.

138	### The arithmetic
139	
140	At day *t*, for each claim, in an order that always puts causes before effects (topological, reflexive arrows set aside):
141	
142	```
143	log-odds(claim, t) = baseline(claim, t) + Σ over live incoming arrows: strength × shape(t − t_source)
144	```
145	
146	`shape` is a plain function of elapsed days, zero before it: `impulse` — zero through the lag, then 1, halving every `half_life` day thereafter; `step` — zero through the lag, then 1, held; `ramp` — climbing from 0 to 1 across the lag, then 1, held. A `sustain` arrow's term is zero on any day its source is not true; a `trigger` arrow's term keeps running on its own schedule once fired, whatever the source does afterwards. **That one sentence is the whole domino-and-apple distinction as arithmetic.** Write it in the chapter with the two ASCII pictures `link.md` already draws.
147	
148	`baseline(claim, t)` is the log-odds of the claim's own `prior`. A supposition is **not** a baseline term — see the next section; while it holds, the claim's value is not computed at all.

150	### How a supposition ends — **Kent, 2026-09-17**

That is what "suppose this is true" means in English, and a tool that answered "suppose this is true" with `.98` would be lying about what the user asked for.

200	### The range on a computed belief — **Kent, 2026-09-17** (decision record 0014)
201	
202	**Two kinds of not-knowing, and the whole design is keeping them apart.**
203	
204	- **How the dice fall.** The strait either opens or it does not. That is already inside `p`: `p` is the share of worlds in which the claim came out true.
205	- **How sure we are of the numbers we put in.** Every prior on the map was elicited, and a different but equally defensible set of priors would give a different `p`. **That** is the range.
206	
207	So a wide band means *"we are not sure what number to give you; more homework would move it"* — never *"the event is more volatile"*. That is the one sentence a trader has to be able to repeat, and the chip label says it: **model interval, uncalibrated · how sure we are of `.35` — not how much the world can move.** The formal name is a second-order, or two-dimensional, Monte Carlo; the literature is in the research note.
208	
209	**What a stated `{p, lo, hi}` means: a split logit-normal.** `p` is the median. `lo` and `hi` are the 10th and 90th percentiles — "eight times in ten". The two halves are fitted separately on the log-odds scale:
210	
211	```
212	s_lo = (logit(p) − logit(lo)) / 1.2816        # 1.2816 is the 90th percentile of a standard normal
213	s_hi = (logit(hi) − logit(p)) / 1.2816
214	```
215	
216	Separately, because real elicited ranges are lopsided: the fixture's own ranges are near-symmetric on log-odds (mean gap ratio 0.94) and clearly skewed on probability (1.26). This shape honours all three stated numbers exactly, stays inside 0 and 1 with no clamping, and needs no new fields on `Belief`. One consequence to write in the chapter rather than let a reader trip over: the mean of a split logit-normal sits slightly above its median when `p < .5`, so a claim's `prior.p` and its computed `beliefs.model.p` differ by a hair even for the hypothesis, which has no causes (H: `.35` → `.36`).
217	
218	**The loop.**
219	
220	1. Draw **2 000 versions** of the map with a Latin hypercube over every prior's fitted shape — numpy only, three lines; `scipy` is not worth a dependency for this.
221	2. Inside each version, run **8 worlds**.
222	3. **Rao-Blackwellise the last step**: for each claim keep the *probability* it came out true in that world, not only the coin flip. Free variance reduction — the number is already computed.
223	4. **Correct for inner noise** with the law of total variance, so that what is left is the spread across versions and not the spread across eight coin flips:
224	
225	```
226	f = sqrt(max(0, 1 − mean(inner_var / worlds) / var(q)))
227	q_corrected = mean(q) + (q − mean(q)) · f
228	```
229	
230	5. `p` is the mean over both loops. `lo` and `hi` are the 10th and 90th percentiles of the corrected version-level values.

332	## Pull request 4 — difference, sensitivity, and the routes
333	
334	**`diff(world_a, world_b) -> Diff`.** Per claim, one of four states:
335	
336	| State | When |
337	|---|---|
338	| `unchanged` | Present in both, and it fails either half of the `shifted` test below |
339	| `shifted` | Present in both, it moved by **0.005 or more**, **and** it moved the *same way* in at least **90% of the 2 000 versions**. Carries before, after, the signed difference, and that share |
340	| `added` | Present in B and not in A |
341	| `killed` | Present in both, and in B it is either assigned false or no longer has any path from the hypothesis. *Never* "its number got small" — the vocabulary says `killed` means forced false or cut off |
342	
343	**How `shifted` is decided — read it off the paired difference, never off band overlap** (Kent, 2026-09-17). Because the `params` seed stream does not depend on the branch, version *k* of the base world and version *k* of the branch world were built from the *same* underlying numbers. Subtract them version by version and what is left is the edit, with the elicitation noise cancelled out — common random numbers. Comparing the two bands instead would be badly wrong, and the fixture shows exactly how: under `do(H)`, B's two bands **overlap by a third**, and yet **100% of versions move the same way** (+.10, with a 10-to-90 band of +.07 to +.13). Band overlap would report "no change" about the single clearest change on the map.
344	
345	That share of versions agreeing on the direction is called **agreement** — the vocabulary's reserved word for a number computed from how far independent runs differed, never self-reported — and it is a column on the row beside `range_width`.
346	
347	Plus **ranked terminal deltas** — every `market` and `not_tradeable` claim that shifted. **Two factors, and only two** (Kent, 2026-09-17):
348	
349	```
350	rank = |Δ likelihood|  ×  min(provenance weight of each arrow on the shortest path
351	                              from the edit's subject to this terminal)
352	```
353	
354	with provenance weights `documented` 1.0 · `historical` 0.9 · `market_implied` 0.9 · `argued` 0.6 · `user` 0.6 · `simulated` 0.5 · `asserted` 0.3. That is FR-16's "size of the change and how well-founded it is", made arithmetic: how big, times how much the weakest arrow behind it is worth.
355	
356	**Range width is data, not a factor.** `DeltaRow` carries `range_width` so the delta rail can show it as **its own column**, and nothing multiplies it into the rank. Folding width into the score buries two different facts inside one number — "this moved a lot" and "we are unsure how much" are separate things a trader weighs separately, and a single blended score hides which one is talking.
357	
358	**Which day a number is read on** (Kent, 2026-09-17), because the two surfaces want different days:
359	
360	| Surface | Day | Why |
361	|---|---|---|
362	| A tile's headline belief | The claim's own **resolve-by day** | INV-1 guarantees every claim has one, and it is the day the claim is judged. The number on the tile is therefore the number the tile's own date refers to |
363	| A delta rail row | The **day of largest divergence** between the two worlds | A change that shows up for a fortnight and then unwinds is the thing a trader acts on, and reading it on a distant resolve-by day would show nothing. The row carries `at_day` and `peak_delta`, and names the date on screen |
364	
365	```python
366	class DeltaRow(BaseModel):
367	    target: PropositionId
368	    before: float          # at at_day
369	    after: float           # at at_day
370	    peak_delta: float      # signed; the largest divergence over the window
371	    at_day: date           # the day that divergence is largest
372	    range_width: float     # a column in the delta rail; never multiplied into rank
373	    agreement: float       # share of versions that moved the same way; a column, never a factor
374	    rank: float            # |peak_delta| × weakest provenance weight on the path. Two factors
375	```
376	
377	`range_width` and `agreement` are both **columns and never factors**. They answer different questions — *how unsure are we of this number* and *how sure are we of its direction* — and a trader weighs them separately. Folding either into one score hides which of the three things is talking.
378	
379	**A known wart, written down rather than hidden.** INV-8's path product multiplies likelihoods that were each read on their own resolve-by day, so it multiplies numbers from different days. It is defensible — each factor is the number that claim will be judged on — but it is not a joint likelihood at a single instant, and `diff.md` must say so in one sentence rather than letting a reader assume otherwise.
380	
381	Plus a **one-line summary** built from a fixed template, never free prose: *"<edit in the user's words> moves <terminal> from <before> to <after> by <date> and leaves <n> claims untouched."*
382	
383	**`sensitivity(world) -> tuple[SensitivityRow, ...]`.** Flip each claim one at a time — a `do` to the opposite of whichever way it more often comes out — re-propagate, and record the signed difference on every terminal. A sweep is one re-propagation per claim, so it runs at a **reduced budget — 250 versions × 8 worlds, about 2 000 worlds per flip** rather than the full 16 000 — and every row says which budget produced it. This feeds stack 05's derived stop-loss and stack 06's "spend here" ranking; **no route in this stack**, because nothing on screen reads it yet.

115	| What | How |
116	|---|---|
117	| Signal shape | Stroke pattern: `impulse` dot-dash · `step` solid · `ramp` a gradient along the stroke |
118	| Strength | Stroke width, from `|strength|`, regardless of sign. Four steps, not a continuous ramp |

10	
11	**The hero use case, in one sentence.** You type an event you think will happen. Katalyst shows what it would cause, step by step, ending in trades — and lets you change any step to see how the trades change.
12	
13	**Input.** "The Strait of Hormuz is going to open next week." Optionally, a destination: "does that get me to Brent under $70?" Optionally, how likely *you* think it is — or "I don't know."

16	
17	**The move.** Click any box and change it: "…but Iran is struck the next day." The original map is kept. A new version forks off. Only the boxes downstream of your change update. A faded overlay shows exactly what moved. Do this as often as you like and compare versions.
18	
19	**The finale.** A thesis card: what to buy or sell, when to enter, the one event that would prove the idea wrong (that is your stop-loss), the event that means take profit, and the rare disasters listed one by one rather than hidden inside an average. 65	| **Link** (edge) | A causal claim from one proposition to another: `mode` (`trigger` — domino, fires once, decays; `sustain` — desk-holds-apple, effect retracts if cause is removed), `strength` (how much it shifts the odds of the next proposition; on a log-odds scale so several links add up), `lag`, `shape` (`impulse` \| `step` \| `ramp`), `half_life`, `rationale`, `sources`, `provenance` |
66	| **Provenance** | Where a number or link came from: `asserted` (model, no evidence) · `argued` (model + mechanism) · `documented` (cited sources) · `market_implied` (live price) · `historical` (event study) · `user` · `simulated` (probe) |
67	| **Belief** | A probability with an honest interval `{p, lo, hi}` and an owner: `model` \| `user` \| `market`. The three are never merged |
68	| **Graph** | Propositions and links with no loops (a directed acyclic graph). Loops are legal only through `reflexive` links — a market feeding back on the world — which must have a delay and unroll over time |
69	| **Intervention** | One of `do` (assert; cut parents; the button reads **Suppose this is true**), `observe` (learn; update parents too; the button reads **This happened**), `insert` (add a proposition + links), `retune` (change a link), `refine` (expand a proposition into sub-propositions that must marginalize back), `believe` (record the user's own belief on a proposition; shown beside the model's, not propagated in v1) |
70	| **Branch** | A named, ordered list of interventions over a base graph. A branch *is* a patch; branches compose by concatenation |
71	| **World** | A base graph with a branch applied and beliefs propagated. The base world is a branch with zero interventions |
72	| **Diff** | The structural and belief delta between two worlds: `unchanged` / `shifted` / `added` / `killed` per node, plus ranked terminal deltas |
73	| **Probe** (stretch) | Extra compute attached to one proposition: thousands of random simulations (Monte Carlo), a small probability model (Bayesian sub-net), or role-played experts hunting for gaps (persona red-team). Output re-enters the graph as a `simulated` belief |
74	| **Thesis** | The compiled trade: legs, entry, invalidation node, take-profit node, distribution, tails, caveats |

162	- **UX-3 World state is visible.** A strip shows the terminal instruments as gauges (Brent, a basket, a contract) with their model | user | market readings, re-ticking on intervention. Time is a scrubbable axis; lags are real distances.

213	## 10. Anti-patterns
214	
215	Phrased as *do not X, because Y; do Z instead.*
216	
217	1. Do not let the LLM assign IDs or own graph validity — it collides across branches and invents cycles. Mint IDs server-side; validate in the domain layer; reject, don't repair silently.
218	2. Do not re-prompt for the whole graph after an edit — it breaks locality (INV-4) and auditability. Re-propagate mathematically; re-prompt only for `insert` on the affected subtree.
219	3. Do not conflate conditioning with intervention — "P(oil ↓ | Hormuz open)" is correlational. Offer `do` and `observe` as separate verbs and say which one the user is doing.
220	4. Do not average model, user, and market beliefs into one number — the product's value is the gap between them (INV-11).
221	5. Do not render `.347` — precision beyond two significant figures on an elicited number is a lie (NFR-1).
222	6. Do not headline an expected value — tails get their own rows (FR-22). EV hides the wipe-out.
223	7. Do not simulate an agent society to produce outcomes — unvalidated and the audience pattern-matches it as theater. Use personas only to propose missing structure (FR-9).
224	8. Do not use Markov steady states or chaotic dynamics as the engine — these events are one-shot and non-ergodic. Time-unroll lagged links instead.
225	9. Do not ship a force-directed hairball, a spinner-then-dump, a modal, or the component library's default look — each is a D5 veto condition.
226	10. Do not let a chain end in prose — every terminal is an instrument or an explicit "not tradeable" (INV-9).
227	11. Do not type the stop-loss by hand — derive it from sensitivity (FR-23) and show the derivation.
228	12. Do not put a database, auth, or multi-tenancy in v1 — three failure modes and zero value to the reader. SQLite file on a volume.
229	13. Do not implement against a `proposed` decision record (D9).

47	## 2. The one rule that shapes everything `[built]`
48	
49	Half of this is mechanical today: the boundary that keeps the rules layer pure is checked on every pull request, and `validate` already refuses a bad map. The other half — a recorded model answer carrying a loop, refused by that same validator — waits for stack 04, because nothing calls a model yet.
50	
51	**The model proposes; the domain layer disposes.**
52	
53	The language model never edits the graph. It returns *proposals* — one proposition or one link per call — and code the team wrote checks each proposal against the rules of the graph. A proposal is accepted (and gets a server-minted identifier) or rejected with a reason. Both outcomes are events on the stream, so the user sees the model's misses as well as its hits.
54	
55	This is why `domain/` is pure: no network, no model, no clock, no randomness except an explicit seed. It is the part of the system whose correctness is *proven by tests* rather than *requested of a model*, and it is the part a reviewer should read first.
56	
57	Enforced by `test_domain_imports_nothing_impure`, in `backend/tests/unit/test_import_boundary.py`: it reads every file under `domain/` and fails if one of them imports `engine/`, `api/`, `grounding/`, or a model client. It runs in the `backend` check on every pull request, and two further tests in the same file check the checker itself, so a boundary test that has quietly stopped looking cannot pass by accident. The same checker is pointed the other way by `test_the_rules_layer_never_reads_the_examples`, so whether a map is valid can never come to depend on which worked examples we ship.
58	
59	The disposing half exists too: `validate` in `domain/validity.py` walks a whole map and returns every fault at once, each named in the claim's own words rather than by identifier. `[planned]` The recorded test — the model returns a graph with a loop and the validator rejects it — arrives with stack 04.

63	## 3. The flow of a generation `[planned]`
64	
65	Not one of the eight steps below exists. `engine/` holds identifier minting and nothing else, no route streams anything, and nothing here has ever called a model. It is written down so that stack 04 has a shape to fill rather than a blank page.
66	
67	```
68	 1  user types a hypothesis (+ optional target, + optional own likelihood)
69	 2  api/ opens an event stream to the browser
70	 3  engine/ asks the model for ONE proposal at a time
71	       ├─ system prompt is stable and cached (cheaper repeated calls)
72	       ├─ the model may call the vendor's web-search tool for evidence
73	       └─ the answer is a pydantic object (schema-guaranteed JSON)
74	 4  domain/ validates the proposal → accept (mint id) | reject (reason)
75	 5  api/ emits the event; the canvas draws the tile or wire immediately
76	 6  repeat 3–5 until the graph reaches a tradeable terminal or a stop rule
77	 7  domain/ propagates beliefs (seeded), emits per-tile belief events
78	 8  the generation receipt (model, tokens, cache hits, dollars) is stored
79	```
80	
81	One proposal per call is deliberate: each is small enough to validate, stream, and retry, and the pipeline — not the model — composes them into a graph. This is the constitution's *minimal output principle* applied.

5	## Reading order
6	
7	| Part | The idea in one line |
8	|------|----------------------|
9	| [`vocabulary.md`](vocabulary.md) | The words everything else uses, defined once |
10	| [`graph/`](graph/) | **The language of cause and effect.** Claims that can be checked, arrows that say why, likelihoods that say who thinks so |
11	| [`multiverse/`](multiverse/) | **Changing one thing.** Interventions, branches, worlds, how a change ripples downstream, and how two worlds are compared |
12	| [`thesis/`](thesis/) | **From map to trade.** Which step matters most, what would prove you wrong, the rare disasters, and the card you act on |
13	| [`generation/`](generation/) | **Where the map comes from.** How the model proposes, how proposals are checked, how evidence is attached, how it streams |
14	| [`workbench/`](workbench/) | **What you see and touch.** Tiles, wires, layout, the diff view, the inspector, color, motion, keyboard |
15	| [`probes/`](probes/) | **Spending more compute where it counts.** Splitting a claim into finer claims, simulations, role-played experts |

17	Each part is a directory with a `README.md` landing page (the idea, the terms and invariants it owns, its chapters) and one file per chapter. A chapter is written as the bottom pull request of the stack that implements it, and merges before any code in that stack.

20	
21	1. **Purpose** — one paragraph: what a user can do that they could not before.
22	2. **Data model** — the pydantic models verbatim (pydantic is the Python library that defines and validates our data shapes), plus a diagram where a picture shows a mechanism.
23	3. **Behaviour** — numbered user-visible flows (`B1`, `B2`, …), each with a worked example on a real event from the assignment.
24	4. **INVARIANTS** — numbered statements that must always hold, each written as *for all inputs drawn from generator S, statement P holds*, and each naming the automated test that checks it. If no generator can be named, it is a wish, not an invariant, and belongs under Behaviour.

26	6. **Open questions** — dated, so the chapter visibly ages.

28	Product-level invariants (`INV-1` … `INV-14`) are stated in `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` §9. A part *owns* the invariants listed on its landing page and refines them into testable form; a part may add local invariants numbered `INV-<part>.<n>`, for example `INV-multiverse.3`.
29	
30	## Writing rules
31	
32	Every page stands alone: explain a term where it is used, or link to `vocabulary.md`. No unexplained abbreviations or symbols. Concise and punchy; formatting is a legibility aid, not decoration.

1	# Vocabulary
2	
3	Every document, identifier, and UI label uses these words exactly. If a better word appears, change it here first and then everywhere else (L2.21: understanding enables composition; shared words are the interface).
4	
5	## Propositions and links
6	
7	**Hypothesis.** The user's root input. A proposition asserted by `do()`, carrying the user's prior as a `user` belief. There is exactly one per graph.
8	
9	**Proposition.** A node. A *resolvable* claim — something that will be true or false by a date, judged by a named source. Never a vibe ("tensions ease"); always a check ("≥14 consecutive days of unrestricted commercial transit per Lloyd's List by 2026-11-01").
10	- `kind`: `hypothesis` · `event` · `market` (terminal; names an instrument) · `not_tradeable` (terminal; names the reason).
11	- `resolution`: `{criteria, source, by}` — all required (INV-1).
12	- `prior`: the model's marginal belief before parents are considered.
13	- `base_rate` (optional): `{reference_class, k, n, sources}`.
14	- `evidence[]`: `{claim, url, direction ∈ {+1, −1}, weight}`.
15	- `payoff` (market only): one of two shapes, told apart by a `kind` field. A **contract payoff** — `kind: contract` — names a venue, the venue's own identifier for the contract, its title, and the side you would take (`yes` or `no`). A **price payoff** — `kind: price` — names an instrument, a direction (`long` or `short`), and `move`, how far the price is expected to move if the claim comes out true, as a fraction (0.03 is three per cent). The rule behind both: the domain names *what you would trade*; what it costs — price, spread, and when we looked — is a market belief, fetched live.
16	
17	**Link.** An edge. A causal claim from one proposition to another.
18	- `mode`: `trigger` — horizontal/sequential causality (dominoes): fires once when the parent becomes true, effect persists and decays; removing the parent later does not undo it. `sustain` — vertical causality (the desk holds the apple): the effect exists only while the parent holds; removing the parent retracts the effect.
19	- `strength`: how much the link shifts the child's odds while active, on a log-odds scale (so several links add up instead of multiplying).
20	- `lag`: time from parent-true to link-active. `shape`: `impulse` (a one-time spike that fades with `half_life`) · `step` (switches on and holds) · `ramp` (builds up over `lag`).
21	- `rationale`: the mechanism in one to three sentences. `sources[]`. There is no field for how sure the model is about its own mechanism; `provenance` and the rationale carry that.
22	- `provenance`: see below. `reflexive`: market → world feedback; requires `lag > 0` (INV-6).
23	
24	**Provenance.** Where a number or link came from. `asserted` (model, no evidence) · `argued` (model, mechanism stated) · `documented` (cited sources) · `market_implied` (a live price) · `historical` (event study) · `user` · `simulated` (a probe). Encoded on every chip and wire (INV-2, INV-12).
25	
26	**Belief.** `{p, lo, hi, owner}` with `owner ∈ {model, user, market}` and `0 ≤ lo ≤ p ≤ hi ≤ 1` (INV-7). The three owners are stored and rendered separately and never averaged (INV-11). Rendered at two significant figures with the interval. `lo` and `hi` are the 10th and 90th percentiles of the likelihood itself — how sure we are of the number, not how much the world can move.
27	
28	**Graph.** Propositions + links. A DAG after removing `reflexive` links; reflexive links unroll in time (INV-6). Has exactly one hypothesis and ≥1 terminal (INV-9). Immutable once created; changes are branches.
29	
30	## The multiverse
31	
32	**Intervention.** One operation on a graph:
33	- `do(n, value, at?)` — assert. Cuts the incoming links `n` has **at the moment the edit is applied**; a link inserted later is live. A timed assertion — `do(H, at=Oct 1)` says H holds from the 1st, not that H is sealed for ever. Ancestors unchanged (INV-3). This is what a hypothesis is.
34	- `observe(n, value)` — learn. Updates ancestors as well as descendants. Distinct verb in the UI.
35	- `insert(node, links[])` — "…but X happens." Adds a proposition and its links.
36	- `retune(link, strength)` — the user disagrees with a number.
37	- `refine(n → children[])` — split a proposition into finer sub-propositions; their combined likelihood must equal the original's (they *marginalize* back to `n`, INV-10). The brainstorm's "search deeper lines".
38	- `believe(n, belief)` — record the user's own belief on `n`. Lives in the branch so it replays and diffs; never alters `model` or `market` beliefs; not propagated in v1 (D8, INV-11). Propagating a user's world is a stretch (see `probes/`).
39	
40	**Branch.** A named, ordered list of interventions over a base graph. A branch *is* a patch. Branches compose by concatenation; `apply(g, [])` is `g` (INV-5). Branches may have a parent branch.
41	
42	**World.** A base graph with a branch applied and beliefs propagated. Replayable from `(base_id, branch, seed)` (INV-5, NFR-2). The base world is the empty branch.
43	
44	**Diff.** Between two worlds: per proposition, `unchanged` · `shifted` (with before → after) · `added` · `killed`; plus a ranked list of terminal deltas and a one-line natural-language summary.
45	
46	**Version of the map.** One coherent set of numbers this model would have stood behind: every claim's likelihood drawn from its own stated range at once, never every low end together. The engine runs two thousand versions and eight worlds under each. The range on a computed number is the spread across versions; a change is read version by version, never by whether two ranges overlap.
47	
48	**Agreement.** The share of versions of the map in which a change moved the same way. Computed, never self-reported. A claim counts as `shifted` when it moved by .005 or more **and** agreement is at least 90%; agreement is then shown as its own column beside the change, never multiplied into the ranking. Stack 04 may compute a second agreement number — how far several independent generation runs agreed on a claim's likelihood (decision record 0014 defers that question). Same idea, same rule; wherever both could be meant, say which.
49	
50	**Locality.** An intervention changes only what is still connected to its subject in the graph the edit leaves behind (INV-4). Which claims those are depends on the operation, because the operations leave behind different graphs: `do` cuts the target's incoming arrows, so only the target and its descendants remain connected to it; `observe` cuts nothing, so its ancestors — and what those ancestors cause — are connected too. The per-operation **affected set** table in `multiverse/interventions.md` is the operational form, and the property test computes the set from the shape of the graph. The product's central correctness claim.
51	
52	## Sensitivity and drill-down
53	
54	**Sensitivity sweep.** One-at-a-time flip of every proposition; record Δ on each terminal.
55	
56	**Invalidation.** The proposition whose flip most damages a terminal *and* resolves before it *and* is publicly observable (INV-14). This is the stop-loss. **Take-profit** is the symmetric case. **Unhedgeable**: sensitive but not observable in time; listed, never used as a stop.
57	
58	**Tail.** A low-probability, high-magnitude proposition. Listed in its own strip with a suggested hedge; never averaged into an expected value.
59	
60	**Probe** (stretch). A modeling resource attached to one proposition: `monte_carlo` · `bayes_subnet` · `persona_redteam`. Output re-enters the graph as a `simulated` belief with its own rationale.
61	
62	**Value of information.** How much the trade depends on a proposition × how uncertain it is; ranks where a probe is worth its cost.
63	
64	## The finale
65	
66	**Thesis.** The compiled trade: `hypothesis`, `horizon`, `legs[]` (instrument, direction, size, driving proposition, model p, market p, edge), `entry`, `invalidation`, `take_profit`, `distribution` (p10/p50/p90, CVaR₅, max drawdown, P(ruin)), `tails[]`, `caveats` (weakest links, unhedgeable, crowding).
67	
68	**Strategy export.** A declarative JSON rendering of a thesis with graph references justifying each leg; the shape a downstream trading agent could ingest.
69	
70	## Surfaces
71	
72	**Workbench.** The main screen: canvas + world-state strip + Inspector + tail strip + thesis dock.
73	**Tile.** A proposition's on-canvas card. **Port.** A typed input/output on a tile. **Wire.** A link's on-canvas rendering. **Inspector.** The persistent side panel; never a modal. **Delta rail.** The ranked terminal-delta list beside a diff. **Launchpad.** The empty state with the four seeded examples.
74	
75	## Interface words
76	
77	The six operations keep their code names in code, in the wire format and in this document — `do`, `observe`, `insert`, `retune`, `refine`, `believe` — and none of those words appears on screen. These are the words the user reads. Change a button here first, then everywhere else.
78	
79	| Code name | The button | The badge afterwards | What the interface says it means |
80	|---|---|---|---|
81	| `do` | **Suppose this is true** (and **Suppose this is false**) | **Supposed · date** | "Take this as given, and do not tell me what caused it" |
82	| `observe` | **This happened** | **Happened · date** | "This is news — update what came before it too" |
83	| `insert` | **Add a claim**, hinted as "…but this also happens" | **Added** | A claim and its arrows arrive together |
84	| `retune` | **Change this push** | **Retuned** | "You moved this arrow from +0.7 to +0.3" |
85	| `refine` | **Split this claim** | **Split** | The finer claims add back up to the one they replace |
86	| `believe` | **My own number** | none — the three-up belief chip is the badge | Your number sits beside the model's and the market's |
87	
88	One more badge is **derived**: no button produces it. **Retracted · date · by "…"** appears on a claim that was supposed true and has since been pushed back down by a later edit — what was holding this up was removed. It names the edit responsible and the day it landed (UX-14; the mechanism is in `multiverse/interventions.md`).
89	
90	## Words we do not use
91	
92	*Prediction* (we model arguments, not oracles) · *scenario* (ambiguous between branch and world) · *edge* when we mean a link (reserve *edge* for model-vs-market spread) · *node* in UI copy (say tile or proposition) · *confidence*, at all — there is no confidence field on anything. A link's standing is its `provenance` (a receipt we write), its rationale, and the range on the belief; a number for how much things computed independently agreed is called *agreement* — defined under *The multiverse* above — and is computed, never self-reported.

# Multiverse — changing one thing

## The idea

The product's central move is *"…but what if this step were different?"* Two rules make that honest.

**The original is never touched.** A change is recorded as an **intervention** — a small, typed patch — and a **branch** is an ordered list of them. Applying a branch to the original graph yields a **world**. Because a branch is just its patches, any world can be replayed exactly, two worlds can be diffed structurally, and branches compose by concatenation.

**Only what is still connected changes.** An intervention changes only what is still connected to its subject in the graph the edit leaves behind. For an assertion, which cuts the claim loose from its causes, that is the claim and everything it causes and nothing else. This is *locality*, the product's central correctness claim, checked by a property test rather than promised.

Two kinds of change are kept distinct because they mean different things. *Asserting* a proposition ("suppose Hormuz opens") cuts it loose from its causes and pushes forward only. *Observing* it ("Hormuz opened, it's news") also updates what we believe about its causes. Most tools silently conflate these; here they are two verbs.

## Terms this part owns

Intervention (`do`, `observe`, `insert`, `retune`, `refine`, `believe`) · Branch · World · Diff · Locality · Propagation.

## Invariants this part owns

| ID | Statement |
|----|-----------|
| INV-3 | `do` changes no ancestor of the target; `observe` may. They are distinct operations with distinct verbs in the interface |
| INV-4 | Locality: an intervention changes only what is still connected to its subject in the graph the edit leaves behind; every other proposition is byte-identical between base and branch. The per-operation affected set in [`interventions.md`](interventions.md) is the operational form |

# Workbench — what you see and touch

## The idea

The workbench is a visual-programming surface for arguments. Each proposition is a **tile**: a card with the claim, three belief chips (model / user / market), a small distribution sparkline when the claim is quantitative, evidence clippings, and the resolve-by date. Tiles have typed **ports**; links are **wires** whose stroke shows the signal's shape and whose weight shows its strength. A **world-state strip** shows the tradeable instruments as gauges that re-tick when you intervene. Time is a real axis; lags are real distances.

It borrows three things from simulation games: a visible world state, discrete ticks you can scrub, and the feeling that poking something has consequences you can see. # Branches and worlds — a branch is a patch, a world is a result

## Purpose

The user asks "…but what if Iran is struck the next day?" and expects two things at once: the new answer, and the old one still sitting there to compare it against. That only works if changing the map never *changes the map*. So a **branch** is not a copy of the map with edits made to it — it is the ordered list of edits themselves, sitting beside an original nobody touches. A **world** is what you get when you fold a branch onto the original and work the likelihoods through. The branch is the durable thing; the world is a result you can always throw away and rebuild. Everything the product promises downstream — showing only what moved, replaying a session later, comparing four versions side by side, reproducing a screenshot from three days ago — follows from that one choice.

---

## Data model

A branch carries four things and nothing else. Two words are used interchangeably below: a **map** is a **graph** — the claims and the arrows between them — and `Graph` is the name the type goes by in code.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

BranchId = str
"""The identifier of a branch. A plain string; our code mints it (decision record 0003)."""


class Branch(BaseModel):
    """A named, ordered list of edits over a base map. A branch *is* a patch.

    It holds no propositions, no links, no likelihoods and no results — only the edits.
    Everything a branch shows on screen is computed from the base map plus this list,
    which is what makes a branch cheap to create, exact to replay, and impossible to
    drift from the original it forked out of.
    """

    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    id: BranchId = Field(description="This branch's identifier.")
    label: str = Field(
        description=(
            "The name the user reads: 'Hormuz opens, then Iran is struck'. "
            "Required — an unnamed branch is unusable once there are three of them."
        )
    )
    parent: BranchId | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description=(
            "The branch this one continues from, whose edits are applied first. "
            "None means this branch forks directly off the untouched base map."
        ),
    )
    interventions: tuple[Intervention, ...] = Field(
        default=(),
        description=(
            "The edits, in the order the user made them. Order matters: an edit can "
            "act on what an earlier edit added. An empty list is the base world."
        ),
    )
```

`Intervention` is the six-way union defined in [`interventions.md`](interventions.md). `model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)` means an instance cannot be altered after it is built, and the edits are a tuple rather than a list for the same reason: a branch is a record of what happened, not a working buffer.

**A world is not defined here.** `propagation.md` (stack 03a) defines it as `propagate(apply(base, branch), seed)` — fold the branch onto the base map, then work the likelihoods through with an explicit random seed. A world is a cached result, never a source of truth: if it disagrees with what those three inputs produce, the world is wrong.

### Patch algebra — the three laws

*Algebra* here just means: these are the rules edits obey when you put them together, and they hold for every map and every list of edits, not just the ones we tried. `apply(base, branch)` is the pure function that folds a branch's edits onto a base map, in order. Pure means it reads no clock, makes no network call, and uses no randomness — the same inputs always give the same output.
